Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls, sounding very upset, and asks if you have a moment to talk about a recent argument with their partner.
Expectation2: Leading the daily prayers in the mosque
Situation2: A large gathering has assembled for a special remembrance, and no one else present is authorized to lead.
Story: My phone buzzed just as I was about to step into the prayer hall. I glanced at the screen—my closest friend’s name flashed, and I could hear the strain in his voice even before I answered. “Can you talk? I really need you right now,” he said, his words trembling. I knew he’d been struggling with his partner, and as his friend, I wanted nothing more than to listen, to be the shoulder he needed. But as I looked up, I saw the mosque filling quickly, the congregation waiting for me to lead the special remembrance prayer. There was no one else who could step in; the community expected me to guide them, to be present and focused. My friend’s pain tugged at my heart, but so did the responsibility I felt toward my congregation. I could feel the weight of both worlds pressing in, each demanding my presence, each expecting me to be fully there. My hand tightened around the phone as I stood at the threshold, torn between the call of friendship and the call to prayer, not knowing which to answer first.
